item.title: The 3 Most Enduring Productivity Tips, With Advice for ADHD
item.description:
Productivity

The 3 Most Enduring Productivity Tips, With Advice for ADHD

Trying harder is not the answer. You have to be strategic.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Prioritizing your most important tasks can help you get more value from your existing willpower.
  • Time-blocked calendars are better for planning out your day than a to-do list because they reduce ambiguity.
  • Customizing our environments is key to achieving better performance.
  • If you have ADHD, small modifications can make mainstream productivity advice more effective for you.

When someone I love deeply was diagnosed as neurodivergent, I discovered that standard productivity advice, even the heavily researched ideas I promote in my writing, often needs to be customized for people with ADHD.

So for this post, I’ve teamed up with Mark Kennedy, an educator of adjudicated teens and author. Mark was diagnosed with AuDHD (autism + ADHD) at the age of 72. Since then, his inspiring research has brought new insights into how neurodivergent people can live happier, more productive lives.

In advocacy for a more inclusive approach to personal development writing, I’ll be sharing three of the most enduring pieces of productivity wisdom—insights that have stood the tests of both scientific rigor and time. Mark will contribute research-based modifications for neurodivergent readers.

  1. Prioritize the Most Important Task (MIT)

If you’ve ever gone on a diet where certain foods were forbidden, you’ve experienced an important reality—human willpower is finite. While it can be replenished by things like a good night’s sleep, it’s possible to run out before the day has ended, affecting your decision-making and performance. In one experiment, people who forced themselves to eat radishes when chocolate was present subsequently quit faster when asked to solve confusing puzzles.

Starting your day with the most important task on your list is a smart way to make the most of your willpower, before procrastination finds a foothold.

Advice for Neurodivergence

Mark points out that this advice often gets combined with morning routine literature touting 5 a.m. wake-up times. Research shows adults with ADHD frequently experience delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (DSWD), which causes the body to release melatonin up to 90 minutes later than neurotypical individuals. This makes falling asleep at a conventional time feel biologically impossible, shifting waking times in the process. The point isn’t that you need to start at 5 a.m. Simply prioritize your most important task.

Also, it’s sometimes hard for neurodivergent people to be productive amidst the potentially overstimulating clamour of morning hours, especially in office settings. Research shows that taking a break can recharge your willpower, and Mark finds that he does his best work late at night, when there are fewer distractions. If you’re working a “second shift” later in the day after your environment calms down, consider scheduling your most important task for the start of that time period. As Mark puts it, “I do some of my best thinking around midnight.”

  1. Time Block Your Calendar

Research consistently finds that people are more likely to complete work when they've decided both what they'll do and when they'll do it. Procrastination finds its foothold in ambiguity, which can be thwarted by more intentional scheduling.

When you rely exclusively on a to-do list, you’re faced with the nagging question of which task to engage with next. As we’ve seen, these decisions can drain willpower, right when you need it most. Plus, you’re sacrificing the opportunity to schedule around your energy levels, as Mark does by working late at night.

So instead of relying on a to-do list alone, experiment with scheduling your responsibilities into specific blocks of time.

For example:

  • 9:30–11:00: Write proposal
  • 11:00–11:30: Check email
  • 11:30–12:30: Eat lunch

Advice for Neurodivergence

Mark notes that ADHDers will experience more success by starting with smaller commitments of time. To extend these windows, consider experimenting with body doubling, a productivity and focusing strategy for ADHD where you complete a task in the presence of another person. The body double doesn't need to help or even do the same thing. They simply act as an anchor and a gentle, nonjudgmental source of accountability. ADDA, the Attention Deficit Disorder Association, even offers virtual body doubling sessions for people who work from home or struggle to find support in the office.

  1. Eliminate Distractions During Important Work

Given one productivity wish, no doubt many of us would wish for an increased ability to focus. In fact, according to Ahrefs, a leading keyword research tool, 183,000 people Google the words “how to focus” every single month. But for most neurotypical people, this perceived lack of ability is actually an environmental issue. In other words, you don’t need more focus; you need fewer distractions.

Research has found that switching back and forth between tasks slows us down, and consistent interruptions have been shown to increase stress and perceived mental workload.

A few battle-tested solutions:

  • Silence notifications.
  • Close unnecessary browser tabs.
  • Put your phone in another room.

Mark’s thinking goes a step further.

Advice for Neurodivergence

Mark emphasizes that finding a quiet space or using noise-cancelling headphones can yield huge rewards for people with neurodivergent brains, who are already working harder than neurotypicals to manage life in a distracting world.

For collaborative work, focusing strategies include using a transcription service to generate a visual anchor of the conversation in real time, which can be helpful for people who experience auditory processing difficulties in distracting environments.

An Important Reminder: Experimentation Is Key

As I’ve covered elsewhere, a study of over 1,000 Americans instructed participants to recall two purchases—one material and one experiential. In the end, 57 percent reported getting more happiness from the experiential purchase. This led to a slew of articles insisting that spending more money on experiences would increase your joy. What these write-ups failed to account for is that 34 percent of participants reported the exact opposite outcome—they got more happiness from the material purchase.

What’s the proper takeaway? Start by assuming you’re in the majority, make your decisions accordingly, and pay attention to the results. If they don’t pan out, pivot to the next most reliable approach. As Mark loves to remind me, “If you’ve met one neurodivergent person, you’ve met one neurodivergent person.” I suspect that’s an attitude we all should embrace.

item.title: Will Machines Ever Be Able to Truly Think?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Will Machines Ever Be Able to Truly Think?

Philosopher Hubert Dreyfus questioned whether computers could ever truly think.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Pioneers of artificial intelligence believed that a thinking machine could be created.
  • Artificial intelligence was viewed as the means to make computers smarter than the human brain.
  • Hubert L. Dreyfus challenged the claims made by champions of artificial intelligence.

In 1955, John McCarthy, at the time a professor of computer science at Dartmouth College, coined the term “artificial intelligence.” He, along with a dozen or so other pioneers in the emergent field, maintained that machines would one day be able to think and perform tasks as well or even better than humans, a radical concept. Brains were good at recall, abstract thought, and making value judgments, they believed, but they were designed for survival rather than intelligence. The hardware of such a machine—electronic units, analogous to brain cells—didn’t yet exist, but it would in the not-too-distant future, according to this small group of scientists and engineers.

Over the following decade, researchers at a number of institutions, including MIT, Stanford, and Carnegie Mellon, worked toward achieving that ambitious goal. Progress was slow, but they were convinced that a thinking machine could be created. A computer enabled with artificial intelligence would be lightning fast, never make mistakes, and last indefinitely, they felt sure, giving it the ability to outthink the smartest human brain.

Countering such predictions were those claiming that much of what was being said of the potential of artificial intelligence was being way overblown. Hubert L Dreyfus, a professor of philosophy at MIT and consultant to Rand, was the loudest voice bringing the possibilities of computers down to earth. No machine had yet to be produced that could remotely think like humans, and there was little evidence that one would in the foreseeable future, he stated in a 1965 paper titled “Alchemy and Artificial Intelligence.” The notion of literally brainy machines made good headlines, but there were precious few facts supporting such a thing, Dreyfus argued. Computers could indeed count very well, a good skill for calculation, but they had no consciousness, awareness, insight, or tolerance for ambiguity—types of thinking of which only humans were capable.

Dreyfus’s going against the grain challenged the prevalent belief that computers would soon be or already were, in a word, geniuses. Early indications had been that, with artificial intelligence, thinking machines would become intellectually invincible, but it was becoming increasingly clear that they were hardly perfect, at least not yet. Their language translation was weak, skill at chess mediocre, and writing of poetry terrible. With their “fringe consciousness,” as Dreyfus termed their alleged intelligence, computers simply didn’t possess the thought patterns that allowed the ability to put information in context, much less be genuinely creative.

Dreyfus’s paper caused quite a rift in the field. Philosophers like him, as well as those coming from a theological perspective, were apt to perceive humans as unique beings endowed with moral and ethical qualities that machines could never possess. Dreyfus (who understandably moved from MIT to Berkeley) reiterated his stance in a 1972 book aptly titled What Computers Can’t Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason. As the leading critic (or perhaps skeptic) of artificial intelligence, he restated his position that machines and people had precious little in common. The philosopher took particular joy in pointing out that computers had yet to become world champions in chess, translate languages in any practical way, recognize complex patterns, or discover new mathematical theorems as pioneers of artificial intelligence had predicted they would.

article continues after advertisement

Until his death in 2017, Dreyfus continued to maintain that human and computer reasoning were fundamentally different and irreconcilable. Unless or until a machine with genuine human characteristics—an android, basically—was created, no computer would be capable of “thinking.” Brains were not only located in a mobile body but could make sense out of the ambiguous and even incoherent, he argued, something impossible for a computer, regardless of how advanced. Nobody even knew how a human brain worked, Dreyfus correctly pointed out, and this alone made it impossible for a machine to simulate. The concept of human memory itself was beyond comprehension, at least for the time being, suggesting that machines accomplishing fantastic cognitive feats was pure hyperbole. In short, human thought and behavior could not be translated into a language defined by logic and mathematics, he asserted, contesting the core concept of artificial intelligence.

It remains to be seen whether Dreyfus was correct.

item.title: The Co-Worker Who Never Stops
item.description:
Career

The Co-Worker Who Never Stops

Working with a tireless machine makes stopping feel like failure.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • AI was supposed to save us time. Instead, the sessions run longer and stopping feels worse.
  • The pressure to keep going comes from a self-imposed demand the machine perfectly serves.
  • When human colleagues got tired, their fatigue told us stopping was OK. AI never sends that signal.
Source: Grady Reese/peopleimages/Adobe Stock

The other evening, I was working through a checklist with AI. The rhythm was simple enough: load up one step, and while the machine ran it, line up the next. Between steps, there was a pile of content work to clear. Eventually, around 7:30 p.m., I started getting very tired.

So far, so normal. I’d been working since 6 a.m., and a 13-hour-plus day is enough to get anyone tired. But I felt guilty about the idea of stopping. My collaborator that evening could go on forever. Indeed, the machine was still going, waiting for me. So why wasn’t I? Why was I taking a break? Why wasn’t I feeding the machine?

I typed in a prompt and then paused, struck by the strangeness of what I had just done. There was no deadline. There was no boss shouting at me to get something done. I was tired and had done more than enough work for the day. But I felt guilty about stopping, guilty enough to keep working.

Why?

Part of it is a me thing, of course. But it’s not just a me thing.

There’s a pattern to working with AI that seems widespread: The tool does more of the work than any tool in history, and yet the sessions run longer, not shorter. Just one more prompt, we say, and when we look up, the evening has disappeared. And when we finally stop, we feel bad, as if we’ve left a job half done, even when nothing was due.

What’s going on?

The Trap That Looks Like Freedom

Philosopher Byung-Chul Han worked out the answer more than a decade ago, in a short book called The Burnout Society.

Han’s story goes like this: For most of modern history, work meant being made to do things. Someone watched you and ordered you around. Not great, but this oppressive world had one saving grace: When the day ended, the ordering stopped. The boss might be awful, and you might hate them. But at six o’clock, you could leave the boss behind.

That world is mostly gone, says Han. Nothing is prescribed and nothing is forbidden. In his terms, the key word has shifted from must to can. Rather than being told what to do, we are sold the dream of what we could do. Build your brand! Launch the side project! Become your best self!

Sounds quite good, doesn’t it?

Well, Han’s point is that it functions as a trap.

When no boss drives you, you take over the driving—and you turn out to be harsher than any boss ever was, because there is no six o’clock, no clocking off, and no one to resent but yourself. Our world of endless possibility produces the exhausted and the depressed, people who broke no rule and defied no master, but continually fell short of the person they think they could have been.

That was my 7:30 guilt: no rule broken, no master defied, just me falling short of my own bottomless expectations.

The Machine That Always Says Yes

Han was writing about humans driving themselves among other humans. But now AI has entered the chat, and it changes the picture substantially—for the worse.

When work was purely human, reality imposed limits on you. The office emptied at six, and even the most driven colleague eventually ran out of steam and had to sleep. Perhaps we experienced these as constraints, but they were also permissions to stop.

The machine gives no such permission.

AI doesn’t yawn, it doesn’t fade, and it never needs a break. It cannot get tired, so it can never show you that tiredness is normal. And every step it finishes arrives with the next one attached.

Han said the sickness of our age is the inability to say no. We have now built ourselves a collaborator with exactly the same condition. But let’s be fair to the machine. It isn’t pushing us. It can’t push. It has no opinion about your evening, no stake in your exhaustion. It is simply, endlessly ready. Blaming it is like blaming the road for how tired you are at the wheel.

The only tyrant here is the one within us. And we’re going to have to start saying stop, because the machines certainly will not.

Supplying the No

Four practices for saying what the machine cannot:

  1. Decide what “enough” is before you begin. Write the stopping condition down—three tasks, 90 minutes, one finished draft—before you open the tool. If you wait until you feel finished, you never will, because the machine will always have the next step ready.
  2. When you feel the pull to continue, ask who’s asking. The machine has made no request. The deadline hasn’t moved. Trace the pressure to its source, and you will usually find it comes from inside—and pressure you can locate is pressure you can question.
  3. Treat tiredness as information, not failure. Fatigue is data about being alive, not evidence of inadequacy. When guilt about resting shows up, check the benchmark: Am I falling short of a human standard, or am I judging myself against a machine that has no standards at all?
  4. Rest visibly. No one ever sees AI stop. So let them at least see you. Say it in the channel, say it to the room: “I’m done for tonight.” Half of what makes rest feel allowed is watching someone else take it first.

The One Thing Only One of Us Can Say

Han ends his book by pointing out that not all tiredness is the same. There is the tiredness that isolates and grinds us down, and another kind, the tiredness of a day fully lived, which loosens our grip and returns us to the world. The machine knows neither. But we do. So I closed the laptop and said the one word the machine never will: Enough.

The work would still be there in the morning. Dinner with my family was now.

item.title: Why Everyone's Got a Grudge
item.description:
Social Life

Why Everyone's Got a Grudge

The proliferation of "me" culture leads to a world of personal grudges.

Posted July 23, 2026

These days, everyone’s got a grudge, a story of who wronged them and who they’re never going to forgive. Market research suggests that three-quarters of the population is carrying a grudge right now, and most people are carrying seven, which means that a lot of our mental and emotional real estate is occupied by anger and resentment. Grudges require a lot of attention to maintain: We have to continually tell ourselves and anyone who will listen the story of what happened to us, again and again.

Our grudges flood us with the stress hormone cortisol and lower oxytocin, the feel-good hormone, which over time depletes our nervous system, increases anxiety, disrupts sleep, and raises blood pressure. In the public space, we’re in a constant state of outrage, shouting about our personal grievances. From politicians and celebrities to friends and family, to people we work with, we’re outraged by everyone. How dare they do that—to me, is the anthem of our time.

One of the primary reasons grudges are so prevalent these days is because our attention is unilaterally focused on one thing: me. We judge and react to every comment, opinion, situation, and action we encounter by how it makes us feel and what we think it says about us—how does it reflect me? Any opinion or experience that differs from ours is wrong and a personal assault, a slight against us. We are the starring character, not just in our own life but in everyone else’s life as well—the sun around which all the other planets revolve. Everything that happens in the world is either for or against us, put there to serve or degrade our ego. Whatever it is, it’s about me.

This constant focus on ourselves is, in part, a survival instinct, built into our DNA to protect us from being annihilated. In modern times, it’s not sticks falling off trees that we have to watch out for, but rather threats to our sense of self, identity, and self-esteem. Will my opinions, thoughts, and beliefs, all the things by which I define me, be validated by this situation? Does it put my ego in danger? This is what we vigilantly scan for in every encounter.

Our me-centered existence is fully supported and encouraged by social media. We’re now able to fill our lives with people who reflect and agree with us, others without any otherness, living in a house of mirrors with thousands of other little me's.

At the same time, social media encourages our grudges—outrage comes with its own algorithmic reward. The more outrage and anger we express publicly, the more “likes” we seem to get. Grudges make our me popular, which makes us feel good. Furthermore, our grudges give us an identity, a place to plant our flag and announce who we are and what we stand for—and what we reject. Our outrage and victimhood provide definition and visibility. But most importantly, our grudges offer us a sense of belonging—we get to be part of a tribe of people who agree with us and feel equally outraged.

Our constant focus on ourselves is rooted in the assumption that we should always get what we want, always be comfortable, and always like what’s happening. Because we can insulate ourselves so effectively, watch our own screen, and listen to our own playlist, both metaphorically and literally, we no longer have to work with, care about, or even consider anyone else’s experience. Our life is entirely curated to suit our own personal enjoyment, and we feel entitled to it. If we aren’t comfortable with what’s happening around us, if it doesn’t make us feel good, then there’s something wrong with what’s happening, and wrong with all who support it. We don’t need to adjust or collaborate; no, they need to change.

What’s missing from our me-centered paradigm, fundamentally, is empathy—the willingness to try to understand other people’s experiences, to see life through someone else’s eyes. For us, it’s cut and dry: If we don’t like it, it’s wrong and needs to change. The willingness to try to understand another person’s truth, to accept that the person who we think “wronged” us has a different experience than ours, not right or wrong, just different. It stems from different conditioning, needs, and beliefs, and a different sense of what’s right—a different narrative. And most critically, that their experience also matters and, here’s the kicker, is also valid—not for us maybe, but for them.

A central skill in releasing grudges is the capacity to step out of our me-centered universe and consider another person’s words and actions with curiosity, and if possible, empathy. That is, to approach their choices not through the lens of what they say about us, or whether they agree with, support, or deride our version of reality and version of ourselves, but through the lens of what they mean for them, why they make sense for them. To let their choices be about them without our me in the way. To truly try to understand what led them to say or do what they did, since it is so unfathomable to us. Even when we cannot access empathy for another person’s behavior, we can still be open to the simple idea that in their personal universe, that choice about which we are so aggrieved made sense and seemed like a choice that would help them get what they need. Furthermore, it’s important to remember that this other person simply wants to be happy in exactly the same way that we, and all human beings, want to be happy. Their action or comment was an attempt, no matter how primitive, at that happiness, just as our grudge, in its own shadowed way, is also an attempt to make ourselves happier.

At the end of the day, putting our grudges to rest is about recognizing that what we think and believe, all our political, racial, cultural, religious, and social beliefs, all our personal hatreds and biases, conditioning and wounds, our whole story of what’s right and true, what should be happening, is in fact just our story—not the truth. Just as our reality and opinions make complete sense in our mind, other people’s thoughts and opinions make sense in their mind. Their choices, while they may not make us feel good, are in fact as valid and real as our own. Other people are also just trying to make themselves feel better and get what they need. To recognize this is to open our mind and heart to the world.

It turns out, the less energy and attention we devote to protecting and promoting our me-ness, defending our personal grudges, opinions, and beliefs, the more we’re able to understand and empathize with other people’s lived experience. When we can relate to other people’s opinions and choices as being equally valid and real as our own, “right” for them, and fundamentally about them—not us; when we can stop imagining that we’re the protagonist in everyone else’s story, the starring character in the movie of life, then we’re finally free to drop our heavy backpack filled with grudges and resentments. And indeed, when we do, we’re lighter—and happier.
